newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: ENDING S.AFRICA FX CONTROLS TO TAKE 4-5 YRS - STALS.
newsitem.headline: ENDING S.AFRICA FX CONTROLS TO TAKE 4-5 YRS - STALS.

text.p: Dismantling South Africa's foreign exchange controls will be a gradual process which is likely to take four to five years, Reserve bank Governor Chris Stals told Reuters in an interview on Friday.
Stals ruled out the suggestion of a "big bang" -- or one-off -- scrapping of controls and said there were no policy differences between himself and Finance Minister Trevor Manuel.
Ending controls would be linked to implementation of measures outlined in the government's macro-economic strategy, known as GEAR (Growth, Employment and Redistribution), he said.
"These things will be done over the next four to five years. Therefore exchange controls will be dismantled over the next four to five years.

"It's part of the programme. If we we have big inflows of capital next year we can go a lot faster, but that applies to all the other things in that programme. Exchange control abolition is part of the the consistent programme of GEAR and GEAR is a four to five year programme."

Commenting on an interview he gave to Business Day newspaper earlier this week, where he talked about conditions for a "big bang" scrapping of controls, Stals said his aim had been to explain why this option was not feasible.
"I was trying to explain why we cannot have a big bang...The only way to do it is to do it gradually," he said while attending a conference here.
Dealers had been wrong in trying to detect a split between himself and Manuel or finance director general Maria Ramos, he said:
"Dealers try to create some difference of interpretation which nobody intended."

Stals said he agreed with comments by Manuel and Ramos that some prudential requirements might be needed on local institutions to ensure they had adequate local cover for local liabilities after exchange controls ended.
Low reserves continued to hamper moves to ease exchange controls, and Stals said he would ideally like to have three months import cover in place -- or 30 billion rands.
"But that certainly is not the policy. The policy is a little bit of this, and a little bit of that," he added.

October official reserves rose marginally to 10.28 billion rand from 10.04 billion in September, or four weeks import cover. Including foreign reserves held at commercial banks, Stals said South Africa's total reserves stood at 13-14 billion rand.
